newsitem.title: UK: UK Treasury committee casts doubt on budget forecasts.
newsitem.headline: UK Treasury committee casts doubt on budget forecasts.

text.p: British politicians briefed to keep a particular watch on the economy have cast doubt on elements of the budget unveiled by Chancellor of the Exchequer Kenneth Clarke in November, particularly his plans to cut public spending.
A report released on Tuesday by the UK parliament's Treasury select committee which comprises politicians from all major parties said the budget was a broadly balanced tax package.
But it said the government's aim to reduce public spending to below 40 percent of gross domestic product over time could be optimistic.
"It may be that a tighter fiscal stance could have improved the outlook for public borrowing and possibly inflation in the medium-term," the report said.
It said the government's assumption that inflation will remain low and stable while GDP growth will continue to rise ran right through the its proposals but was by no means certain to happen.
"We are concerned that any failure to achieve rising GDP output combined with falling inflation as expected in the current plans could jeopardise the credibility of fiscal and monetary policy."

Higher-than-expected inflation would force up interest rates and squeeze the public sector borrowing requirement as government departments' spending allotments are eroded in real terms, leading to pressure for them to be increased.

The committee also placed a question mark over the government's plans to crack down on benefit fraud and save nearly 7.0 billion pounds ($11.72 billion) over three years in the process -- the so-called "spend to save" scheme.
"We are concerned that there is a risk that modest increases in expenditure on "spend to save" will not yield the forecast large increases in receipts over the planning period," it said.
The scheme will cost 800 million pounds, Clarke said.

A failure to meet his seven billion target would also put pressure on the government's PSBR forecast. The government has pencilled in a figure of 26.4 billion pounds this financial year, falling to 19.2 billion next year.

The report said the government's control spending total -- the nominal amount of money it sets itself to spend -- had been boosted by cash flows, notably from the sale of armed forces married quarters and the student loan book, thereby front-loading receipts.
"This has effectively retimed expenditure and receipts so that the current year and next three years benefit, but the longer-term receipts will be reduced," it said.
But all was not doom and gloom for the Chancellor as the committee concluded that a broadly balanced budget had probably helped to keep economic growth on track.
"It is clear that the spending plans remain broadly on course compared to the previous budget, and that despite some slippage in the PSBR, it is still on a downward course."
